content.text:
Your answers pin the target. Here is the closed-out diagnosis — **no code was changed**.

## Confirmed target vs. current behaviour

| Your intent | What the code does today | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **Latest mode** — Metacritic-first, window controlled by `max_date` (or `max_pages` when `max_date: 0`) | Exactly that mechanism — but `max_date` is a **floor**, not a "latest" switch. The sweep starts at the top of the floor year and walks *down* page by page, resuming at a cursor, and only resets when the whole floor range is done. With `max_date: 202601`, `max_cycle_months: 1`, it is ~866 cached 2026 pages, ~16 pages per cycle: a slow crawl through the year, not "look at what's new". | **No concept of "only the newest N games"** — nothing stops after the first pages of the current month. `max_date` bounds how *old* it goes; it does not bound how *deep* it crawls within the window. |
| **Backlog mode** — walk a backlog, check each game exists on FitGirl/FreeGOG | Exists: sweep window → queue → verify → source lookup. | Works structurally, but the queue is a graveyard (1,555 pending, 1,534 below thresholds, 16,896 expired all-time) and the source lookup is blocked (below). |
| **Sort by critic/user score** | `sort_order` is **order only**, never a filter; and in `criticscore`/`userscore` there is no year dimension, so `max_date` is ignored there (logged each cycle). | If score should *filter*, it can only happen at detail verification — browse scores are Metacritic's internal metrics (~1168), not 0–100. |
| **Explicit mode switch** | No mode concept: behaviour is an emergent consequence of `max_date`, `max_pages`, `max_cycle_*` and `sort_order`. | Needs `mode: latest | backlog` (or equivalent) so intent is declarative. |
| **Filter before queueing** | Queue first, verify later. Pending is the holding pen, so below-threshold games occupy it for 30 days and are re-checked from cache every cycle ("1555 checked, 21 passed, 1534 kept"). | Verification must move **before** insertion, and below-threshold games must not be held. |

## The three defects that explain what you're seeing

**1. `hv` substring kills ~all deliveries (dominant).** `_title_contains_keywords` is a plain substring test over the whole FitGirl article body. Real page (Black Myth: Wukong) contains *"Only updated files for a new **non-HV** repack"* and *"convert your INSTALLED **HV** version"* — conversion-patch notes — so the token `hv` matches. Evidence: 7,821 skips on `hv` (+ 1,817 `emulator`, 771 `hypervisor`) across the log; **all 21 verified games** (Wukong, Metaphor, RE Requiem, Forza Horizon 6, Crimson Desert, JWE3…) blocked; **63 delivered vs 9,490 failed vs 16,896 expired** all-time. Your answer: keep the intent, fix the matching — so the fix must be whole-word plus negation-aware (`non-HV`, `without HV`), and/or scoped to the repack title + "Repack Features" rather than the full body.

**2. "Latest" is a slow crawl, not a look at what's new.** The 2026 listing is 866 cached pages deep; a cycle advances ~16 pages and mostly re-sees known slugs — *"3 of 800 collected games passed title/age filters"*. New releases appear on page 1 only, are picked up once, then dedupe permanently excludes them. So you see no new games even though new games *are* on page 1 every day.

**3. Old games arrive in bursts.** What escapes the keyword blocker is typically a 2024/2025 title queued weeks earlier that finally matched; the last delivery batch (28 on Nov 5) was FF XVI, Dragon Ball Sparking! Zero, Red Dead Redemption, Romancing SaGa 2 — all ~2024. Expiry waves (276 on Oct 30, 110 on Nov 1) explain the "no pattern" feeling.

## What needs changing (the change list, no code yet)

1. **Keyword matcher** — whole-word, negation-aware, and scoped to title + requirements/features; add a regression test using a real "non-HV repack" article.
2. **Explicit `mode`** — `latest` (shallow: newest pages of the window, e.g. first N pages / current month only, then stop) vs `backlog` (deep: cursor-driven sweep to the floor). Plus the existing `sort_order` applying to both.
3. **Filter before queueing** — queue only games that already pass detail thresholds; below-threshold games are dropped (or held ≤1–2 days), not 30. This alone drains the 1,555-strong queue.
4. **Window semantics made honest** — document/encode that `max_date` is a floor and add a depth control for latest mode (pages-per-cycle *and* a "stop after the newest month" rule), so "latest" cannot degenerate into a year-long crawl.
5. **Score filtering** — decide explicitly that critic/user score filters at verification, and that sort order only re-orders (which is what the code already does) — or make score mode bound the queue as well.

Nothing has been modified. If you want to proceed, the natural next step is a design spec for these five changes (then a fix chain) — say the word and I'll write it to `docs/agent/specs/`.


| Property | pi |
| ---------- | ---- |

| `harness.path.skills` | `plugins/.../skills/` |

---

## Part 2: Dispatch & User Prompts

### Subagent Dispatch — Mode Selection

The dispatch tool has two modes. Pick exactly one — never mix parameters.

| Mode | Use when | Key parameters |
|------|----------|----------------|
| **SINGLE** | One agent, one task | `agent`, `task`, `model` |
| **WORKFLOW** | Multiple agents, parallel/sequential | Harness dispatch form (below): one entry per agent |


**Correct — SINGLE mode:** invoke the `subagent` tool with `agent`, `task`,
and `model` arguments. No workflow block is needed and the call is never
documentation.

**Correct — WORKFLOW mode (parallel with a same-turn completion barrier):**

A dispatch needs **two separate acts** in one reply. (1) Write this as the
**one** `js workflow` code block, opening the fence at the start of a line (no
indentation). (2) Invoke the `subagent` tool with `workflow: true` and
`async: true` as a **real tool call**.

Writing `subagent(...)` in a code fence, an inline span, or prose produces
documentation only: it starts nothing, returns no workflow ID, and leaves every
child unstarted while the reply still looks correct. Reproducing the shape of an
example is not dispatching.

```js workflow
const results = await runs.all([
  { key: "a", agent: "implementer", task: "Do X", model: "${harness.model.implementer}" },
  { key: "b", agent: "implementer", task: "Do Y", model: "${harness.model.implementer}" }
]);
return results;
```

Then invoke the `subagent` tool with `workflow: true` and `async: true`. It
returns a workflow ID. A fenced `subagent(...)` line is not that call.

`runs.all` starts both entries in parallel. `async: true` follows the Pi
workflow protocol; the Completion barriers rule below decides whether this turn
waits on that ID or ends and waits natively.


### Dispatch by Harness

**Pi** — apply the Completion barriers rule below before the turn ends;
`runs.all` still runs all entries in parallel. A dispatch needs **two separate
acts** in one reply: (1) write this as the **one** `js workflow` code block,
opening the fence at the start of a line (no indentation); (2) invoke the
`subagent` tool with `workflow: true` and `async: true` as a **real tool call**.

Writing `subagent(...)` in a code fence, an inline span, or prose produces
documentation only — it starts nothing and returns no workflow ID. Reproducing
the shape of an example is not dispatching.

The reply text payload:

```js workflow
const results = await runs.all([
  { key: "reviewer-a", agent: "reviewer", task: "<prompt>", model: "${harness.model.reviewer_a}" },
  { key: "reviewer-b", agent: "reviewer", task: "<prompt>", model: "${harness.model.reviewer_b}" }
]);
return results;
```

Then invoke the `subagent` tool with `workflow: true` and `async: true`. It
returns a workflow ID; apply the Completion barriers rule below to decide
between waiting on it and ending the turn.

#### No workflow ID means the dispatch did NOT happen

| What you observe | Meaning | Required action |
| ----------------- | --------- | ----------------- |
| Tool returned a workflow ID | Launched | `bg_wait` that exact ID before the turn ends (chain step) |
| Tool returned an error | Not launched | Fix the cause, re-invoke the tool |
| No tool result in your turn | **Not launched** — you emitted text | Re-invoke the tool; do not proceed |
| You cannot name the workflow ID | **Not launched** | Re-invoke the tool; do not report success |

Never `bg_wait` a placeholder, guessed, or empty ID. Never report a child as
dispatched, running, or started without a workflow ID from the tool. If repeated
invocations return no ID, stop and tell the user the launch failed — a silent
no-op lets collection and every later chain step run against work that does not
exist.

Key rules:

- `async: true` follows the Pi protocol; `runs.all` remains parallel.
- In a chain step, exact-run `bg_wait` before the turn ends is the completion
  barrier; standalone work waits natively.
- Between launch and the barrier, do not send a progress-only response, invoke
  another skill, or let the chain step end.
- After waiting, inspect terminal status and collect every expected result.
- Re-dispatch individual reviewers on `failed`/`cancelled` before de-duplication.
- Resume the originating review loop or implementation step; never hand its
  unfinished work to a downstream chain step.
- Do NOT use nested `async function` — use top-level `await` only.



### Completion barriers

A dispatch result is a dependency: no dependent work, and no next chain step,
until that result is in hand. Follow the harness-specific behavior above;
independent entries remain parallel.

**Inside a chain step** — a prompt-template step (`/chain-*`, a `chain:`
template, or any step whose end advances to the next skill, because the step
resolves when your turn ends — keep the turn open:

1. Write the workflow script block and invoke the `subagent` tool with
   `workflow: true` and `async: true` as a real tool call. Capture the exact
   workflow ID from the result; reply text is not a dispatch.
2. Do the independent local work that does not depend on the results (read the
   diff, prepare validation, plan the synthesis).
3. Before the turn can end, call `bg_wait` on that exact ID with
   `stopOnAttention: false`.
4. Consume every result only once the run is terminal with all expected results.
   A wait that returns earlier — window elapsed, work still active — means call
   `bg_wait` again on the same ID.
5. Resume the originating loop, never a downstream skill.

**Standalone work** — an ordinary chat with no chain step involved — has no
turn-level dependency: end the turn and let the native completion wake the
session. Do not call `bg_wait` merely to wait, and do not report results you
have not received. Use `bg_wait` standalone only for provider, detached, or
other background work with no native notification, or when a skill contract must
produce a same-turn artifact.

If a wake never arrives (a session reopened in a new process), read the result
with `subagent({ action: "status" })` instead of re-dispatching.

| Rationalization | Required behavior |
| ----------------- | ------------------- |
| "The async dispatch call itself means this chain step is complete." | A launch is not a barrier; wait on the exact workflow ID before the step can end. |
| "I wrote the `subagent(...)` call in my reply, so the workflow is launched." | Reply text is not a tool call. If no tool returned a workflow ID, nothing launched — re-invoke the tool. |
| "The dispatch looked correct, so the children are probably running." | Only a returned workflow ID proves a launch. Without one, re-invoke before any dependent work. |
| "In a chain step, native completion notifications are the waiting mechanism; do not poll." | Wrong there: the step resolves when the turn ends, so the chain advances and the result lands inside the next step. Call exact-run `bg_wait`. |
| "I'll report the complete results when the native workflow completion notification arrives." | Not inside a chain step. Wait on the exact run before letting the step end. |
| "I should call `bg_wait` in every chat, to be safe." | Standalone work has native completion. Waiting there is dead time and hides that the turn could have ended. End the turn. |
| "I must wait immediately — no other tool between launch and wait." | Independent work that does not need the results runs first. The barrier blocks dependent work and turn-ending, not useful work. |
| "I can report that review is running and let tech-debt or QA continue." | A live review must reach its terminal status before dependent work runs. |
| "Waiting will serialize the two reviewers." | `runs.all` stays parallel; the wait only blocks dependent parent work. |

**Red flags:** ending a result-dependent chain step after an `async: true`
dispatch, treating a fenced `subagent(...)` line as a dispatch, advancing without
a workflow ID returned by the tool, calling `bg_wait` in standalone work that has
native completion, reading "standalone" into a step whose end advances the
chain, waiting for the wrong run, omitting `stopOnAttention: false`, sending a
progress-only response while a chain step is active, or invoking
tech-debt/QA/finalising before the live review reaches terminal status.


### User Prompts

**Pi (`ask_user_question`):**

```typescript
ask_user_question({
  questions: [{
    header: "<Max 16 chars>",
    question: "<The question text>",
    options: [
      { label: "<Option label>", description: "<What this option means>" }
    ]
  }]
})
```

- `header`: max 16 characters.
- `options`: 2–4 per question. Each needs `label` and `description`.
- Multi-select: add `multiSelect: true`.



---

## Part 3: Environment Configuration

### Authentication Flows

Applies to every `aws`, `gh`, and `az` command, including one you only run to
check something.

| Provider | pi (home) |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| GitHub / Git | MCP-handled |
| AWS | — |
| Azure | — |



### MCP Server Routing

`context7` is the preferred source for library/framework docs. Retry once on connection errors; if still failing, tell
user to run `/mcp <name>`.

| Server | pi | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `github` | ✅ | Repos, PRs, issues, branches, commits, code search, Actions |
| `context7` | ✅ | Up-to-date npm/Python library and framework docs |


### Commit/Push Rules

The finalising skill references `harness.commit.mode` to determine options.

| Rule | pi (home) |
| ------ | ----------- |
| `harness.commit.mode` | `automated` |
| Push to default branch | Allowed |
| Version bump | Auto-detect semver |
| PR merge | Auto squash-merge |
| GitHub release | Auto-create with tag |
| Branch cleanup | Preserve |


**automated (home/pi):** bump → (if not on default: PR + squash-merge) → push → release → preserve branch.


**Dynamic options (finalising skill):**

- **review-required:** Create PR, Keep, Discard
- **automated, on default:** Bump+Push+Release, Keep, Discard
- **automated, on feature branch:** full flow with PR merge and release
</skill>

invocations return no ID, stop and tell the user the launch failed — a silent
no-op lets collection and every later chain step run against work that does not
exist.

Key rules:

- `async: true` follows the Pi protocol; `runs.all` remains parallel.
- In a chain step, exact-run `bg_wait` before the turn ends is the completion
  barrier; standalone work waits natively.
- Between launch and the barrier, do not send a progress-only response, invoke
  another skill, or let the chain step end.
- After waiting, inspect terminal status and collect every expected result.
- Re-dispatch individual reviewers on `failed`/`cancelled` before de-duplication.
- Resume the originating review loop or implementation step; never hand its
  unfinished work to a downstream chain step.
- Do NOT use nested `async function` — use top-level `await` only.



### Completion barriers

A dispatch result is a dependency: no dependent work, and no next chain step,
until that result is in hand. Follow the harness-specific behavior above;
independent entries remain parallel.

**Inside a chain step** — a prompt-template step (`/chain-*`, a `chain:`
template, or any step whose end advances to the next skill, because the step
resolves when your turn ends — keep the turn open:

1. Write the workflow script block and invoke the `subagent` tool with
   `workflow: true` and `async: true` as a real tool call. Capture the exact
   workflow ID from the result; reply text is not a dispatch.
2. Do the independent local work that does not depend on the results (read the
   diff, prepare validation, plan the synthesis).
3. Before the turn can end, call `bg_wait` on that exact ID with
   `stopOnAttention: false`.
4. Consume every result only once the run is terminal with all expected results.
   A wait that returns earlier — window elapsed, work still active — means call
   `bg_wait` again on the same ID.
5. Resume the originating loop, never a downstream skill.

**Standalone work** — an ordinary chat with no chain step involved — has no
turn-level dependency: end the turn and let the native completion wake the
session. Do not call `bg_wait` merely to wait, and do not report results you
have not received. Use `bg_wait` standalone only for provider, detached, or
other background work with no native notification, or when a skill contract must
produce a same-turn artifact.

If a wake never arrives (a session reopened in a new process), read the result
with `subagent({ action: "status" })` instead of re-dispatching.

| Rationalization | Required behavior |
| ----------------- | ------------------- |
| "The async dispatch call itself means this chain step is complete." | A launch is not a barrier; wait on the exact workflow ID before the step can end. |
| "I wrote the `subagent(...)` call in my reply, so the workflow is launched." | Reply text is not a tool call. If no tool returned a workflow ID, nothing launched — re-invoke the tool. |
| "The dispatch looked correct, so the children are probably running." | Only a returned workflow ID proves a launch. Without one, re-invoke before any dependent work. |
| "In a chain step, native completion notifications are the waiting mechanism; do not poll." | Wrong there: the step resolves when the turn ends, so the chain advances and the result lands inside the next step. Call exact-run `bg_wait`. |
| "I'll report the complete results when the native workflow completion notification arrives." | Not inside a chain step. Wait on the exact run before letting the step end. |
| "I should call `bg_wait` in every chat, to be safe." | Standalone work has native completion. Waiting there is dead time and hides that the turn could have ended. End the turn. |
| "I must wait immediately — no other tool between launch and wait." | Independent work that does not need the results runs first. The barrier blocks dependent work and turn-ending, not useful work. |
| "I can report that review is running and let tech-debt or QA continue." | A live review must reach its terminal status before dependent work runs. |
| "Waiting will serialize the two reviewers." | `runs.all` stays parallel; the wait only blocks dependent parent work. |

**Red flags:** ending a result-dependent chain step after an `async: true`
dispatch, treating a fenced `subagent(...)` line as a dispatch, advancing without
a workflow ID returned by the tool, calling `bg_wait` in standalone work that has
native completion, reading "standalone" into a step whose end advances the
chain, waiting for the wrong run, omitting `stopOnAttention: false`, sending a
progress-only response while a chain step is active, or invoking
tech-debt/QA/finalising before the live review reaches terminal status.


### User Prompts

**Pi (`ask_user_question`):**

```typescript
ask_user_question({
  questions: [{
    header: "<Max 16 chars>",
    question: "<The question text>",
    options: [
      { label: "<Option label>", description: "<What this option means>" }
    ]
  }]
})
```

- `header`: max 16 characters.
- `options`: 2–4 per question. Each needs `label` and `description`.
- Multi-select: add `multiSelect: true`.



---

## Part 3: Environment Configuration

### Authentication Flows

Applies to every `aws`, `gh`, and `az` command, including one you only run to
check something.

| Provider | pi (home) |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| GitHub / Git | MCP-handled |
| AWS | — |
| Azure | — |



### MCP Server Routing

`context7` is the preferred source for library/framework docs. Retry once on connection errors; if still failing, tell
user to run `/mcp <name>`.

| Server | pi | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `github` | ✅ | Repos, PRs, issues, branches, commits, code search, Actions |
| `context7` | ✅ | Up-to-date npm/Python library and framework docs |


### Commit/Push Rules

The finalising skill references `harness.commit.mode` to determine options.

| Rule | pi (home) |
| ------ | ----------- |
| `harness.commit.mode` | `automated` |
| Push to default branch | Allowed |
| Version bump | Auto-detect semver |
| PR merge | Auto squash-merge |
| GitHub release | Auto-create with tag |
| Branch cleanup | Preserve |


**automated (home/pi):** bump → (if not on default: PR + squash-merge) → push → release → preserve branch.

# Project Context

## Overview

Orient yourself on the current project by using session history, git log, README, and the agent design docs (latest
spec, latest plan, every review ledger). This is a no-op only when the emitted completion marker is present; otherwise,
gather context even if you already know some project details.

**Core principle:** An emitted status marker, not subjective familiarity, determines whether context is loaded.

## Prerequisite: None (Bootstrap Owner)

If the current conversation already contains `Project context status: loaded.`
as an emitted status line, skip this skill and report `Context already loaded.`
Otherwise emit `Project context status: loading.` and continue.
`get-context` is a utility skill: it loads no other skill and owns the context
bootstrap.

**Never load the `harness` skill here.** A missing `Harness status: loaded.`
marker is not a reason to load it; detect the harness inline in Step 2.

**Red flag:** loading the `harness` skill or emitting `Harness status: loaded.`
from within `get-context`.

## The Process

### State Rule

The prerequisite marker is the sole no-op condition. Do not infer that context is loaded from startup files, skill text,
repository familiarity, or partial knowledge.

| Rationalization | Required behavior |
|-----------------|-------------------|
| "I already know the project" | Gather context unless the emitted completion marker is present. |
| "Startup loaded AGENTS.md" | Treat that as partial context, not completed context loading. |

**Red flag:** responding `Context already loaded.` without an emitted `Project context status: loaded.` marker.

### Step 2: Detect Harness (Inline)

Determine which harness you're running under from the cues below (never load
the `harness` skill):

- `subagent()` available → **pi** harness

Announce: `🖥️ Harness: [pi].`

- **pi** harness → follow the Pi path (Step 3a)

### Step 3a: Gather Context (Pi Harness — Total Recall)

#### Calculate Project Slug

```bash
cwd=$(pwd)
path="${cwd#/}"
slug="--${path//\//-}--"
echo "PROJECT_SLUG=$slug"
```

Set `PROJECT_SLUG` from the output.

#### Query Sessions

1. **Find recent sessions:**

   ```text
   session_list(project="PROJECT_SLUG", limit=3)
   ```

2. **Cross-session search:**

   ```text
   session_search(query="architecture decisions recent work changes patterns", project="PROJECT_SLUG", limit=5)
   ```

3. **Read the most substantive session:**

   ```text
   session_read(session="<path from most substantive result>")
   ```

Continue to Step 4 (common context).



### Step 4: Common Context (All Harnesses)

#### Read the Project README

```bash
head -60 README.md 2>/dev/null || echo "(no README found)"
```

If using MCP or with GitHub remote, prefer:

```text
github_get_file_contents(path="README.md", limit=60)
```

#### Repo Facts

Resolve the repository root once -- never assume the current directory is it:

```bash
ROOT="${GIT_ROOT:-$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel || pwd)}"
echo "ROOT=$ROOT"
```

This path has not collected git facts yet:

```bash
git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
git -C "$ROOT" log --oneline -10
```

#### Design Docs (Specs, Plans, Reviews)

Agent-written design docs live under `$ROOT/docs/agent/`. Ignore the legacy
`docs/specs/` and `docs/plans/` trees: they hold superseded designs, not issue records.

| Directory | What to read |
| --------- | ------------ |
| `docs/agent/specs/` | Newest only -- `head -40` |
| `docs/agent/plans/` | Newest only -- `head -40` |
| `docs/agent/reviews/` | Every file, in full |

"Newest" means the highest `YYYY-MM-DD-` filename prefix; on a tie take the name that
sorts last. Rank by filename, not by mtime.

```bash
for family in specs plans reviews; do
  dir="$ROOT/docs/agent/$family"
  [ -d "$dir" ] || continue
  echo "== $family ($(find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.md' | wc -l) files) =="
  find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.md' | sort
done
```

The 40-line read is the opening only: it carries the title, the problem, and any
superseded or status note. A live plan can exceed 80 KB, so the bound is fixed. Reviews
are read in full: each is a review ledger — `<topic>-residuals.md` holds this change's
findings left unverified at the review's round cap, and `<topic>-deferred.md` holds findings
deferred as outside the change's scope. A newer ledger does not supersede an older one.
Those ledgers are the repository's record of known defects.

**Skip rule:** if `$ROOT/docs/agent/` is missing, or a family directory is absent or
holds no `*.md` files, skip that family. A missing directory is not a blocker, risk, gap,
or finding -- never report one, and never create one.

Reading these files is context gathering, not target-file reading: nothing is modified.

### Step 5: Synthesise

Present a concise synthesis in 6-10 bullet points covering
everything you gathered. The goal is useful context without
overloading the window:

- **What is this project?** — repo, branch, CWD, purpose from README
- **What were we last working on?** — session summary, checkpoints
  (initial goal vs actual result), root causes from technical_details
- **What decisions were made?** — capture decision rationale from
  checkpoints' `technical_details` / `root_cause_or_decisions`
- **What's the current state?** — blockers, pending items, what's
  working vs broken from checkpoints' `next_steps` and last turn
- **What changed?** — files created vs edited (from session_files),
  latest commit diff stats
- **Linked artifacts** — PRs, issues, commits from session_refs
- **Git log** — recent commit messages showing what was landed
- **Design docs** — the newest spec and plan (paths plus the direction their opening
  sections describe), and every unresolved finding from the review ledgers with the
  file that records it; when `docs/agent/` is absent or empty there is nothing to
  report here

Include the harness identifier: `🖥️ Harness: [pi].`

**Do NOT include tool output verbatim.** Summarise findings in your
own words. Each bullet should convey meaningful context, not just
a table row.

After completing the context synthesis, emit the status line `Project context status: loaded.`
</skill>

<skill name="create-spec">
# create-spec Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you
understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until
you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived
simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Prerequisite: Harness and Project Context

Before beginning, ensure both prerequisites are loaded:

1. If `Harness status: loaded.` is not already present as an emitted status line, load and run `harness`, then return here.
2. If `Project context status: loaded.` is not already present as an emitted status line, load and run `get-context`,
   then return here.

When invoked from a chain, preserve these status markers and do not repeat either prerequisite.

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple"
projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly
simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a
   clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/agent/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file; this is the terminal step

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph create-spec {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Design doc complete — done" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Design doc complete — done" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is the approved and committed design doc.** Do NOT implement anything yourself. If standalone: stop
here. If in a chain: report completion — the chain handles implementation.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build
  a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining
  details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent
  pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal
  design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and

- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?

# create-spec Ideas Into Designs

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you
understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until
you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived
simplicity.

## Prerequisite: Harness and Project Context

2. If `Project context status: loaded.` is not already present as an emitted status line, load and run `get-context`,
   then return here.

When invoked from a chain, preserve these status markers and do not repeat either prerequisite.

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple"
projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly
simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a
   clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/agent/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file; this is the terminal step

## Process Flow

```dot

    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];

    "Present design sections" [shape=box];

    "Write design doc" [shape=box];

    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
```

=== browse -> pending filter chain ===
def _process_browse_games(
    browse_games: list[dict[str, Any]],
    platform: str,
    db: Database,
    thresholds: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    max_queue_days: int = 30,
    reject_title: list[str] | None = None,
) -> int:
    """Evaluate browse-page games and insert qualifying ones into the pending queue.

    Browse listings from ``_parse_browse_page`` already include scores
    in their dict (``score`` = critic metascore, ``user_rating`` = user
    score).  Games that pass the thresholds are inserted into
    ``pending_games``.  Already-processed or already-pending games are
    skipped.

    Args:
        browse_games: List from ``_parse_browse_page``.
        platform: Target platform name.
        db: Database instance.
        thresholds: Dict with ``min_criticscore`` keys.
        max_queue_days: How many days to keep the game pending before expiry.
        reject_title: Titles matching any of these are skipped.

    Returns:
        Number of new pending games added.
    """
    known_slugs = db.get_known_slugs(source="metacritic")
    new_count = 0
    seen_slugs: set[str] = set()
    for game in browse_games:
        if not _is_game_eligible(game, db, thresholds, known_slugs=known_slugs):
            continue
        if _title_matches_reject(game.get("title", ""), reject_title):
            logger.debug("Skipping '{}' — matches reject_title", game.get("title", ""))
            continue

        reject_reason = _reject_by_browse_review_counts(
            game,
            min_critic_reviews=thresholds.get("min_criticscore_reviews", 0),
            min_user_reviews=thresholds.get("min_user_reviews", 0),
        )
        if reject_reason is not None:
            logger.debug(
                "Skipping '{}' — {}",
                game.get("title", ""),
                reject_reason,
            )
            continue

        g_slug = game.get("slug", "")
        g_title = game.get("title", "")

        # Skip duplicate slugs within this batch — the DB layer would
        # silently no-op, but we avoid the unnecessary roundtrip.
        if g_slug in seen_slugs:
            continue
        seen_slugs.add(g_slug)

        expires_at = _calculate_pending_expiry(max_queue_days)

        db.record_pending(
            slug=g_slug,
            game_title=g_title,
            platform=platform,
            metascore=float(game.get("score") or 0),
            metascore_reviews=game.get("critic_review_count"),
            user_score=float(game.get("user_rating") or 0),
            user_reviews=game.get("user_review_count"),
            release_date=game.get("release_date"),
            expires_at=expires_at,
        )
        new_count += 1
        logger.debug(
            "Added pending game: '{}' (slug: {}, expires {})",
            g_title,
            g_slug,
            expires_at,
        )

    return new_count

def _verify_pending_scores(
    db: Database,
    mc: MetacriticClient,
    platform: str,
    thresholds: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    cache_details_days: int = 7,
    max_verify: int = 50,
    reject_genre: list[str] | None = None,
    reject_title: list[str] | None = None,
    fitgirl_max_queue_days: int = 60,
    notifier: Any = None,
    cancel_event: CancelSignal | None = None,
    sort_order: Literal["new", "criticscore", "userscore"] | None = None,
) -> int:
    """Re-verify pending games' scores against the real Metacritic detail page.

    Browse-page Nuxt data does NOT carry standard 0\u2013100 metascores or
    0\u201310 user scores — the \"score\" fields are internal browse-only
    metrics.  Games whose detail-page scores fail the configured thresholds
    (or cannot be found at all on the detail page) are kept in the queue
    for re-verification on subsequent cycles.

    Games that pass the real-score check have their pending record updated
    with the correct scores from the detail page.

    Only the first *max_verify* games are checked per call; the rest
    remain pending for the next cycle.  This prevents a large pending
    queue (e.g. 2773 games) from generating thousands of sequential
    HTTP requests in a single cycle.

    Args:
        db: Database instance.
        mc: MetacriticClient instance.
        platform: Platform identifier (e.g. ``"pc"``).
        thresholds: Dict with score threshold keys.
        sort_order: Active browse sort order used to order the pending queue
            (see :meth:`Database.get_pending`).  ``None`` keeps the default
            database order.
        cache_details_days: TTL for the detail-page cache.
        max_verify: Maximum number of games to verify per cycle.
            Set to 0 to skip verification entirely.
        reject_genre: List of genre substrings to reject (case-insensitive).
            Games whose genre contains any entry are removed immediately.
            E.g. ``["RPG"]`` matches ``"Action RPG"``, ``"JRPG"``, etc.
        reject_title: List of title substrings to reject (case-insensitive).
            Games whose title contains any entry are removed immediately.
        fitgirl_max_queue_days: Passed through to _process_verify_result for
            expiry recalculation when scores pass.
        notifier: Optional Notifier instance. When provided and every lookup
            in the batch returns None, a scrape notification is sent.

    Returns the number of games removed.
    """
    if max_verify <= 0:
        return 0

    removed = 0
    pending = db.get_pending(platform=platform, sort_order=sort_order)
    total_pending = len(pending)

    # Collect the batch of games to check this cycle
    batch = list(pending[:max_verify])

    if not batch:
        return 0

    removed, any_success = _process_verify_batch(
        db,
        mc,
        platform,
        thresholds,
        batch,
        max_verify,
        total_pending,
        cache_details_days=cache_details_days,
        reject_genre=reject_genre,
        reject_title=reject_title,
        fitgirl_max_queue_days=fitgirl_max_queue_days,
        cancel_event=cancel_event,
    )

    if notifier is not None and not is_cancelled(cancel_event) and batch and not any_success:
        _diagnose_and_notify_scrape(
            notifier,
            _check_scrape_health(),
            "Metacritic game detail lookup failed for all games",
        )

    return removed

def _reject_by_browse_review_counts(
    game: dict[str, Any],
    min_critic_reviews: int,
    min_user_reviews: int,
) -> str | None:
    """Return a rejection reason string if browse-page review counts
    are available and below threshold, or None if the game should proceed.

    Only uses browse-page fields that are real counts (not scaled browse
    metrics).  When a count is None (missing from browse data), the check
    is skipped and the game proceeds to the detail-page verify phase.

    Args:
        game: A browse-page game dict from ``_parse_browse_page``.
        min_critic_reviews: Minimum critic reviews threshold (``min_criticscore_reviews``).
        min_user_reviews: Minimum user reviews threshold (``min_user_reviews``).

    Returns:
        ``"critic_reviews_too_few_at_browse"``, ``"user_reviews_too_few_at_browse"``,
        or ``None`` if the game should proceed.
    """
    critic_count = game.get("critic_review_count")
    if critic_count is not None and critic_count < min_critic_reviews:
        return "critic_reviews_too_few_at_browse"
    user_count = game.get("user_review_count")
    if user_count is not None and user_count < min_user_reviews:
        return "user_reviews_too_few_at_browse"
    return None

Mitigation: a small `rejected_at` memory (a "seen and failed" ledger with a re-check window, e.g. 7-30 days) so failures aren't re-verified every cycle. But the user chose "pass-or-drop ... re-evaluated on the next pass until they either pass or drop off the pages". With `cache_details_days: 7` the lookups are cache hits for a week, then re-fetch. Acceptable, but worth designing: add a lightweight `rejection` memo table or reuse `game_detail_cache` (it already caches detail results by slug with TTL!) — verification consults `game_detail_cache` first, so repeat lookups are cache hits. That's already there (`cache_details_days: 7`). Good: no new table needed; the detail cache absorbs the repeated lookups.

So approach A is viable; the detail cache limits cost.

For the mode switch: single branch in `_run_discovery_phases` (compute `depth_pages` and `use_cursors` from mode), rather than duplicating the year loop. Present as part of design.

content.text:
All eight decisions are locked. Here is the design — five sections; tell me what to change.

## 1. Goal and scope

**The problem, restated from evidence:** deliveries stalled because every FitGirl match is rejected on `hv`/`emulator` found in boilerplate text (7,821 skips, all 21 verified games blocked, 63 deliveries ever); the queue holds 1,555 rows of which 1,534 can never pass (16,896 expired all-time); "latest" is a deep cursor crawl (866 pages of 2026 at 16 pages/cycle), not a look at what's new; and modes are implicit, so behaviour has no predictable pattern.

**Four changes, one spec, sequenced implementation:** (1) keyword matcher, (2) queue migration + verify-before-insert, (3) `mode: latest | backlog`, (4) docs. Discovery stays **Metacritic-first** — no source-first scan is being added.

---

## 2. Config surface

```yaml
review_sites:
  metacritic:
    platform_overrides:
      pc:
        mode: latest        # latest | backlog  (default backlog)
        max_pages: 10       # latest: depth = first 10 pages
                            # backlog: total sweep budget (today's meaning)
        max_date: 202609    # window floor, both modes (0 = no floor)
        max_cycle_months: 1 # backlog pace only (inert in latest)
        max_cycle_pages: 16 # page-mode backlog pace only (inert in latest)
        sort_order: new     # latest REQUIRES "new"; score sorts warn + scan "new"
```

- `mode` is validated as a Literal; default `backlog` preserves today's behaviour, so the migration only adds the key.
- Latest mode: scans **pages 1..N of the window every cycle, no cursors, no reset**; `max_pages` is the depth, and `max_pages: 0` is clamped to 10 with a warning (unbounded latest is just backlog).
- Backlog mode: exactly today's semantics (cursor sweep, `max_date` floor, pacing).
- Inert keys log once per cycle as they do now (`max_cycle_months ignored in latest mode`, etc.).

---

## 3. Discovery pipeline

**Mode resolution** — one predicate, one branch, no duplicated loops:

```
use_cursors = (mode == "backlog")
depth_pages = max_pages                                  # only read in latest
scan_order  = "new" if mode == "latest" else sort_order   # warn when coerced
```

Latest drives the existing year loop with `start_page = 1` each cycle and a hard stop at `depth_pages`; backlog keeps `get_last_scanned_page` / `set_last_scanned_page` and the drained/floor reset logic. Logging changes in latest from `Progress: N of 1000 pages` to `Latest scan: pages 1..N of <window>, M collected`.

**Verify-before-insert** (the chosen approach): inside `_process_browse_games`, each game surviving the cheap filters (known-slug dedupe, `reject_title`, browse review counts) gets a detail lookup via the existing `mc.lookup_game` — which already honours `game_detail_cache` for `cache_details_days`, so repeated cycles are cache hits, not fresh HTTP. `db.record_pending` is then called **only** when the scores pass; it writes the real scores and `score_checks_passed=True`. Games that fail, or have no scores yet, are not inserted — and because unqueued slugs are not marked "known", the next latest-mode pass re-evaluates them automatically.

Two rejected alternatives: a `state` column on `pending_games` (schema change, and the queue still fills with candidates between phases) and a separate `candidates` table (new table, duplicated dedupe logic).

---

## 4. Keyword matcher

`_check_reject_keywords` changes in two ways:

- **Scope:** extract the page `<title>` and the **"Repack Features"** block and match only there. Drop the "truncate at Backwards Compatibility" hack — on real pages it sits at char 2221 and the features block at 4914, so today's truncation discards the authoritative section while keeping the download-mirror boilerplate that causes the false positive.
- **Match rule:** whole-word, negation-aware. `\bhv\b` with a negation window — `non-HV repack`, `without HV`, `no HV support` do **not** match; `HV version`, `requires HV` do.

Measured effect: the Wukong page's two offending sentences (chars 476 and 1027) fall outside the scope entirely, so the game matches again; a genuine HV repack states it in Repack Features and is still rejected.

---

## 5. Queue migration, error handling, testing

- **One-time data migration** (guarded, idempotent, runs once on upgrade): `DELETE FROM pending_games WHERE score_checks_passed IS NOT TRUE`. 1,555 → 21 rows (the verified candidates, including the `hv`-blocked games that will deliver once §4 lands).
- **Error handling:** a detail lookup that fails (network/parse) must not silently drop a candidate — treat it like a failed verification for this cycle and retry next pass (that is what the detail cache + re-read already give us); a missing features block degrades to title-only matching (and logs at DEBUG, never blocks the match).
- **Testing:** unit tests for the matcher (table-driven: `non-HV`, `HV version`, `hypervisor`, missing block), for mode resolution (latest/best-mode matrix, inert-key logs, depth clamp), for verify-before-insert (pass → queued verified; fail → not queued; lookup failure → retried), and for the one-time migration (idempotent, verified rows preserved). Plus a README-accuracy test for the new `mode` row.
- **Out of scope:** source-first scanning of FitGirl/FreeGOG; changing `sort_order` from order-only to filtering; per-mode scheduling intervals; any change to `max_queue_days` semantics for verified rows.

def _fetch_fitgirl_page_content(url: str) -> tuple[str | None, str | None]:
    """Fetch a FitGirl repack page and extract its <title> and <article> text.

    Returns ``(title, article_text)`` where both are ``None`` if the page
    could not be fetched or the tag is missing.  The title has HTML entities
    decoded (e.g. ``'`` → ``'``, ``"`` → ``"``).  The article
    text has HTML tags stripped (including link anchor text from ``<a>``
    elements to exclude download filenames from keyword scanning) and
    whitespace collapsed.

    Returns:
        A ``(title, article_text)`` tuple.
    """
    try:
        # Only fetch from FitGirl (uses self-signed cert — verify=False is intentional)
        if not url.startswith("https://fitgirl-repacks.site"):
            return None, None
        resp = requests.get(
            url,
            headers={"User-Agent": _USER_AGENT},
            timeout=_SITEMAP_TIMEOUT,
            verify=False,
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
    except requests.RequestException:
        return None, None

    html = resp.text
    # Extract <title> tag content
    title: str | None = None
    match = re.search(r"<title[^>]*>(.*?)</title>", html, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL)
    if match:
        title = unescape(match.group(1).strip())

    # Extract <article> text content (excludes sidebar, nav, comments)
    article_text: str | None = None
    article_match = re.search(r"<article[^>]*>(.*?)</article>", html, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL)

arguments.content:
# Design: explicit discovery modes, verify-before-queue, and an honest keyword scope

Date: 2026-11-06
Status: Approved (user agreed each decision in session)

## Goal

Make discovery predictable and stop the queue accumulating games that can never pass.

Three symptoms were reported and then measured against the live instance (867 cycles of
`gamarr.log`, the live `gamarr.db`, and live fetches of FitGirl pages):

1. No new games are delivered, and older games appear only sporadically.
2. The user cannot tell what the daemon is doing, because "mode" is an emergent
   consequence of `max_date` / `max_pages` / `max_cycle_*` rather than a stated choice.
3. The pending queue holds 1,555 rows, 1,534 of which can never pass verification
   (16,896 rows have expired all-time against 63 deliveries).

The intended behaviour is two explicit modes: a **latest** mode that looks at the newest
releases, and a **backlog** mode that sweeps back through older ones, with critic/user
score sorting applying to both.

## What was measured (and what corrected the original diagnosis)

- **The `hv` keyword accounts for most match rejections**: 7,821 skips on `hv`, 1,817 on
  `emulator`, 771 on `hypervisor` in the current log. All 21 games that passed Metacritic
  verification were blocked — Wukong, Metaphor, RE Requiem, Forza Horizon 6, Crimson Desert,
  Jurassic World Evolution 3 and others.
- **Most of those rejections are correct.** FitGirl's "Repack Features" block for Black Myth:
  Wukong reads *"Hypervisor Bypass (INTEL & AMD) by DenuvOwO + Goldberg emu added … Custom
  launcher added for easier HV steps processing"*. Metaphor and Crimson Desert carry the
  same bypass line. These are genuinely HV repacks.
- **A minority are false positives.** Resident Evil Requiem and Forza Horizon 6 have no
  `hv`/`hypervisor`/`emulator` in their Repack Features block; they are rejected on
  download-mirror boilerplate at the top of the page (*"Only updated files for a new non-HV
  repack"*, *"convert your INSTALLED HV version"*).
- **The scope is also upside down.** On the Wukong page the boilerplate sits at characters
  476 and 1027, `Backwards Compatibility` (today's truncation point) at 2221, and
  `Repack Features` at 4914. The current code discards the authoritative section and keeps
  the text that causes false positives.
- **"Latest" is a deep crawl.** The 2026 listing is 866 cached pages; a cycle advances about
  16 pages at `max_cycle_months: 1` and mostly re-sees known slugs (*"3 of 800 collected
  games passed title/age filters"*). Pages 1..N hold the newest releases; the sweep spends
  its time below them.

**Accepted consequence:** the user has confirmed the HV rejection is deliberate.
Denuvo-era AAA titles that FitGirl ships with a hypervisor bypass (Wukong, Metaphor,
Crimson Desert and most new large releases) therefore stay excluded. The keyword change
below fixes the false positives only and is **not** expected to restore AAA delivery.

## Decisions (user-approved)

1. **Latest depth = top-of-window, N pages.** Latest mode starts at page 1 every cycle,
   scans `max_pages` pages, and stops. No cursors, no reset.
2. **Pass-or-drop at queue time.** Verify the detail page before inserting into
   `pending_games`; insert only games that pass. Games that fail, or have no scores yet,
   are not inserted and are re-evaluated on the next pass (unqueued slugs are not "known").
3. **Keyword matching = whole word + negation guard**, scoped to the page `<title>` and the
   **Repack Features** block. The `Backwards Compatibility` truncation hack is removed.
4. **Scope refined after measuring the page layout**: matching only that scope is what
   distinguishes a real HV repack from boilerplate.
5. **`mode: latest | backlog`**, default `backlog`, and `max_pages` keeps its key name:
   total sweep budget in backlog, first-N-pages depth in latest.
6. **Latest requires `sort_order: new`.** A score sort configured with latest logs one
   warning per cycle and scans in `new` order for that cycle; backlog keeps all three sorts.
7. **One-time queue migration**: delete rows where `score_checks_passed IS NOT TRUE`,
   keeping the 21 verified candidates.
8. **One spec, sequenced implementation**: keyword matcher first (removes false positives),
   then queue migration and verify-before-insert, then `mode`, then docs.

## Current mechanics (verified)

- `MetacriticPlatformConfig` (`config.py:112-130`) holds `max_pages` (default 500),
  `max_cycle_pages`, `max_date`, `max_cycle_months`, `sort_order`, `max_queue_days`.
- Discovery is Metacritic-first: `_run_discovery_phases` (`pipeline.py:303`) browses, then
  `_process_browse_games` (`pipeline.py:962`) applies cheap filters — known-slug dedupe
  (`_is_game_eligible`, `pipeline.py:927`), `reject_title`, and
  `_reject_by_browse_review_counts` (`pipeline.py:841`) — and calls `db.record_pending`
  (`database.py:406`). No detail lookup happens here.
- Verification happens afterwards over the whole queue: `_verify_pending_scores`
  (`pipeline.py:1605`), called with `max_verify=len(pending_games)`, so every pending row is
  "checked" each cycle (cache hits via `cache_details_days`). Rows passing get
  `score_checks_passed = TRUE`; failing rows are kept until expiry.
- Matching only processes verified rows: `_match_pending_games` (`pipeline.py:1841`) skips
  `not game.score_checks_passed` (`pipeline.py:1896`).
- `date_mode = bool(cfg.max_date) and cfg.sort_order == "new"` (`pipeline.py:330`) selects
  the date/page branch; latest mode reuses that year loop.
- Keyword rejection: `_check_reject_keywords` (`pipeline.py:2178`) — FitGirl-only
  (`pipeline.py:2173`) — fetches `<title>` + `<article>` text via
  `_fetch_fitgirl_page_content` (`pipeline.py:2974`), truncates at `Backwards Compatibility`
  (`_truncate_at_backwards_compat`, `pipeline.py:2247`), and matches with
  `_title_contains_keywords` — a plain `kw.lower() in text.lower()` substring test.
- Database migrations are additive `ALTER TABLE` statements inside `Database.__init__`
  (`database.py:176`, examples at 215, 265, 270), plus data migrations elsewhere; there is a
  precedent for one-time data changes in the config layer but not yet in the DB layer.
- `scheduler._build_kwargs` (`scheduler.py:313`) forwards the per-platform config to
  `run_acquisition` by explicit key name.

## Design

### 1. Config surface (`src/gamarr/config.py`)

- `MetacriticPlatformConfig` gains `mode: Literal["latest", "backlog"] = "backlog"`.
  Default `backlog` preserves today's behaviour, so the migration only adds the key and users
  keep their current semantics until they opt in.
- No other key changes meaning at the config level. Per-mode semantics are applied in the
  pipeline and documented in the README:

  | Key | `backlog` | `latest` |
  | ----- | ----------- | ---------- |
  | `max_pages` | total sweep budget (today) | depth: first N pages (today's `max_pages: 500` is clamped, see below) |
  | `max_cycle_pages` | per-cycle pace (page mode) | inert |
  | `max_date` | floor of the sweep | floor of the window (informational; depth decides) |
  | `max_cycle_months` | per-cycle pace (date mode) | inert |
  | `sort_order` | all three values | must be `new`; otherwise warned and coerced |

- **Inert-key warnings**: latest mode logs `max_cycle_pages ignored in latest mode` and
  `max_cycle_months ignored in latest mode` once per cycle, matching the existing
  `max_pages … unused in date mode` style (`pipeline.py:311-320`).
- **Depth clamp**: `max_pages: 0` in latest mode means "unbounded", which is just backlog;
  latest clamps `0` to `10` and logs a warning naming both the clamped value and the reason.
  The clamp lives in the pipeline normalisation next to the existing `max_date` /
  `max_cycle_months` guards (`pipeline.py:225-241`), so direct API callers get it too.
- `run_acquisition` and `AcquisitionConfig` gain `mode: Literal["latest", "backlog"] =
  "backlog"`; `scheduler._build_kwargs` forwards it.

### 2. Mode resolution (`src/gamarr/pipeline.py`)

One predicate, one branch. No second copy of the year loop.

```text
use_cursors = (cfg.mode == "backlog")
depth_pages = cfg.max_pages            # latest only, already clamped
scan_order  = "new" if cfg.mode == "latest" else cfg.sort_order
              (warn once per cycle when a score sort was coerced)
```

- **Latest**: for each year in the window (newest first), read from `start_page = 1`, scan
  until `depth_pages` pages have been read across the cycle, and stop. `get_last_scanned_page`
  / `set_last_scanned_page` are not called; `reset_progress` is never called for pacing.
  The date floor from `max_date` still bounds the year range, and the floor/pacing cutoffs
  already implemented (`cutoff_date`, `max_month_span`) apply unchanged.
- **Backlog**: unchanged — cursor sweep, `max_date` floor, `max_cycle_months` /
  `max_cycle_pages` pacing, drained/floor reset.
- **Logging**: latest replaces the page-budget percentage line with
  `Latest scan: pages 1..N of <window>, M collected, K queued`; backlog keeps today's lines.
- The mode is reported once per cycle (`Discovery mode: latest (depth 10 pages)` /
  `Discovery mode: backlog`) so the log always states which mode ran.

### 3. Verify before queueing (`src/gamarr/pipeline.py`)

`_process_browse_games` gains a detail-verification step between the cheap filters and
`db.record_pending`:

```text
for game in browse_games:
    cheap filters (unchanged): eligibility, reject_title, browse review counts
    result = mc.lookup_game(title, platform, cache_details_days, cache_pages_hours)
    if result passes thresholds and has review data:
        db.record_pending(..., metascore=result.metascore, ..., score_checks_passed=True)
    else:
        # not inserted, not marked known -> re-evaluated on the next pass
        log at DEBUG with the reason
```

- **Cost bound**: the cheap filters already reduce ~800 browsed games to a handful of new
  candidates per cycle (measured: 3–11). Detail lookups also pass through
  `game_detail_cache` (`cache_details_days`, default 7), so a game that reappears every cycle
  is a cache hit, not a fresh request.
- **No schema change.** The existing `score_checks_passed` column carries the meaning it
  already has; a row in `pending_games` now always means "verified, awaiting a source match".
- **`_verify_pending_scores` stays** for defensive re-verification of rows that lose their
  verified state (score edits, cache expiry) and for games whose scores were unavailable when
  queued — but its steady-state workload drops to the few verified rows awaiting a match.
- `max_queue_days` keeps its meaning for verified rows (the source-matching window), so a
  verified game that never matches still expires.

### 4. Keyword matcher (`src/gamarr/pipeline.py`)

Two changes in `_check_reject_keywords` and its helpers:

- **Scope**: extract the FitGirl page `<title>` and the **Repack Features** block only.
  The block runs from the "Repack Features" heading to the next section heading. The
  `Backwards Compatibility` truncation is removed (`_truncate_at_backwards_compat` is
  deleted with its call site), because the scope now excludes both the false-positive
  boilerplate above the block and the historical references below it.
  Pages whose features block cannot be found fall back to title-only matching and log at
  DEBUG; they are never blocked on an absent block.
- **Match rule**: whole-word, negation-aware.

  ```text
  match(keyword, text):
      for each \b<keyword>\b occurrence in text (case-insensitive):
          look back over the preceding ~25 characters of the same sentence
          if it ends with "non-", "without ", "no ", "not " -> skip this occurrence
          else -> match
  ```

  Worked examples (from the real pages): `non-HV repack` → no match;
  `Hypervisor Bypass … applied` → match; `easier HV steps processing` → match.
- The rule is implemented as one pure function (text + keywords → matched keyword or None)
  so it is unit-testable without network access.
- **Expected effect, stated honestly**: false-positive pages (RE Requiem, Forza Horizon 6,
  Sonic Racing, Shinobi) become matchable; genuine HV repacks (Wukong, Metaphor, Crimson
  Desert) stay rejected by explicit user decision.

### 5. One-time queue migration (`src/gamarr/database.py`)

- On first open of an existing database, delete rows that can never match:

  ```sql
  DELETE FROM pending_games WHERE score_checks_passed IS NOT TRUE;
  ```

  1,555 rows → 21 on the live instance (the verified candidates).
- Guarded so it runs exactly once: a `PRAGMA user_version` stamp (set to the new value after
  the delete) rather than a heuristic on row counts, so re-opening the database, or a fresh
  database, never repeats it.
- Logged once at INFO: `Queue migration: removed N unverified pending rows (M verified kept)`.
- Documented in the README's migration notes, because it is destructive and surprising:
  a user upgrading mid-sweep loses unverified queue rows (they are re-discovered by the next
  pass, since they were never marked known).

## Error handling

| Condition | Behaviour |
| ----------- | ----------- |
| Detail lookup fails (network/parse) during queueing | Not inserted; retried on the next pass (never marked known) |
| Detail lookup returns no review data yet | Not inserted; retried on the next pass |
| Features block missing on a FitGirl page | Title-only keyword matching, DEBUG log, never blocks |
| `mode: latest` with a score sort | WARN once per cycle, scan in `new` order for that cycle |
| `mode: latest` with `max_pages: 0` | WARN, clamp depth to 10 |
| `max_pages`/`max_cycle_*` set but inert in the active mode | INFO once per cycle, naming the key and the reason |
| Queue migration fails | WARNING, leave the rows, continue; retried on the next open |
| Invalid `mode` value | Config load fails validation with the Literal message |

## Testing

- `tests/unit/test_pipeline.py`
  - Keyword matcher table: `non-HV repack` (no match), `without HV` (no match),
    `Hypervisor Bypass … applied` (match), `easier HV steps processing` (match),
    `hypervisor` inside a word (no match), missing block (title-only), empty keywords.
  - Scope extraction: features block bounded by the next heading; boilerplate above the
    block is not scanned; title always scanned.
  - Mode resolution matrix: latest/backlog × page/date window; latest ignores cursors
    (`get_last_scanned_page` never called); latest stops at the depth; latest warns and
    coerces a score sort; inert-key logs.
  - Verify-before-insert: passes → inserted with `score_checks_passed=True` and real scores;
    fails → not inserted; lookup returns `None` → not inserted and re-attempted next cycle;
    a known slug is still skipped.
- `tests/unit/test_database.py`
  - Queue migration: removes unverified rows, keeps verified ones, records
    `PRAGMA user_version`, does not run twice.
- `tests/unit/test_config.py` — `mode` default and validation; per-platform override.
- `tests/unit/test_scheduler.py` — `_build_kwargs` forwards `mode`.
- `tests/unit/test_readme_accuracy.py` — new `mode` row matches the model default.

## Files

| File | Change |
| ------ | -------- |
| `src/gamarr/config.py` | `mode` field on `MetacriticPlatformConfig` |
| `src/gamarr/pipeline.py` | mode resolution and latest depth; verify-before-insert in `_process_browse_games`; keyword scope + whole-word/negation matcher; remove `_truncate_at_backwards_compat`; mode/depth logging; inert-key warnings |
| `src/gamarr/database.py` | one-time `pending_games` cleanup guarded by `PRAGMA user_version` |
| `src/gamarr/scheduler.py` | `_build_kwargs` forwards `mode` |
| `README.md` | `mode` row, per-mode key meanings, keyword-scope note, queue-migration note |
| `tests/unit/test_pipeline.py`, `test_config.py`, `test_database.py`, `test_scheduler.py`, `test_readme_accuracy.py` | see Testing |

`src/gamarr/metacritic.py` is unchanged: the latest mode reuses the existing year loop,
cutoff handling and detail cache.

## Out of scope

- **Source-first discovery** (scanning FitGirl/FreeGOG for new repacks before Metacritic).
  The user chose to keep discovery Metacritic-first.
- **Accepting HV repacks.** Rejection is deliberate; Wukong/Metaphor/Crimson Desert stay
  excluded. Revisit only as a separate decision.
- Making `sort_order: criticscore` / `userscore` a *filter* rather than an order. Score
  filtering already happens at verification.
- Per-mode scheduling intervals (latest and backlog run from whichever `mode` is configured).
- Changing `max_queue_days` semantics for verified rows.

**What it captures (from your eight answers):**

- **Verify before queueing**: detail lookup between the cheap filters and `record_pending`; only passing games are inserted (`score_checks_passed=True`), failures and score-less games are dropped and re-evaluated next pass. Cost is bounded because the cheap filters already narrow ~800 → 3–11, and `game_detail_cache` absorbs repeats.
- **Keyword matcher**: scope = `<title>` + **Repack Features** block (bounded by the next heading or 4000 chars), whole-word with a 25-character negation guard; the `Backwards Compatibility` truncation is deleted.
- **One-time queue migration**: delete `score_checks_passed IS NOT TRUE` (1,555 → 21 rows), guarded by `PRAGMA user_version` so it runs once.

**One correction recorded in the spec, which changes the expected outcome:** during self-review I fetched the actual pages and the `hv` rejections are *mostly correct* — Wukong, Metaphor and Crimson Desert ship FitGirl's "Hypervisor Bypass" in their Repack Features. Only RE Requiem and Forza Horizon 6 are false positives. Per your decision the rejection stays, so the spec states plainly that AAA HV titles remain excluded and this change only restores the false-positive pages. I'd rather you see that written down than discover it after implementation.

Three self-review fixes applied before committing: the `max_pages` clamp row (only `0` is clamped, not `500`), a bounded end-of-block rule for the features section, and an exact negation window instead of "~25 characters".

<skill name="harness">
# Harness Reference

## Step 0: Detect Harness

Before using any dispatch or prompt syntax, determine which harness you're running under:

| Harness | Dispatch tool | Prompt tool | Dispatch style | Model format |
|---------|-------------|-------------|----------------|-------------|
| **pi** | `subagent()` | `ask_user_question()` | Blocking for dependent workflows | `provider/model:thinking` (e.g. `opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash:high`) |



**Detection:**
- `subagent()` available → **pi** harness
- If your AGENTS.md declares `HARNESS`, use that as confirmation.

Announce: `"🖥️ Harness: [pi]."`

After detecting the harness, emit the status line `Harness status: loaded.`

**Context bootstrap is not this skill's job.** `get-context` owns it: it is the chain
step that follows this one (`prompt-harness -> prompt-get-context`), and any skill
that declares the context prerequisite loads it directly. Do not read project files,
call session tools, or emit a `Project context status:` line here. Never load
`harness` recursively.

| Rationalization | Required behavior |
| ----------------- | ------------------- |
| "I already know the harness" | Require `Harness status: loaded.` as evidence. |
| "Context is missing, so I must load it now" | Not this step. Emit `Harness status: loaded.`; the get-context step owns it. |
| "A missing context marker means this step failed" | The marker is required of the chain, not of this step. Report the harness and stop. |

**Red flags:** claiming the harness without the `Harness status: loaded.` marker,
emitting a `Project context status:` line, reading project files, or invoking
`harness` from within `harness`.

Only a marker emitted by its owning step counts; quoted marker text from merely reading a skill does not.

---

## Part 1: Model & Agent Reference

### Models by Role

| Role | pi (`provider/model:thinking`) | Used by |
| ------ | -------------------------------- | --------- |
| `harness.model.reviewer_a` | `opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash:max` | code-review, pr-review, release-review |
| `harness.model.reviewer_b` | `opencode-go/glm-5.3-flash:max` | code-review, pr-review, release-review |
| `harness.model.fast` | `opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash:max` | quick checks, linting passes |
| `harness.model.implementer` | `opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash:max` | sub-agents, code changes, implementation tasks |



Pi uses `provider/model:level` format — the `:level` suffix sets the thinking level. Valid levels: `off`, `minimal`,
`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`.

### Thinking Levels

**Pi** — already embedded in the model string above. Skills reference only `harness.model.<role>` — no separate thinking
reference needed.




### Agents by Role

| Role | pi | Used by |
| ------ | ---- | --------- |
| `harness.agent.implementer` | `implementer` | sub-agents |
| `harness.agent.reviewer` | `reviewer` | code-review, pr-review, release-review |



In pi each role maps to a builtin agent.

| Rationalization | Required behavior |
| ----------------- | ------------------- |
| "The task needs a planner, so `planner` must be the agent" | Use only listed agent identifiers (the pi registry has no `planner`); dispatch the closest listed role and report the gap. |
| "No binding exists for this role, so I'll reuse another role's model" | Omit `model` so the builtin inherits the session model, and report the gap. |

**Red flags:** dispatching an agent identifier absent from the table (for
example `planner`), or borrowing another role's model when a binding is missing.

### How to Use

After Step 0, set local variables from the tables above:

```text
# Models
REVIEWER_A_MODEL = harness.model.reviewer_a
REVIEWER_B_MODEL = harness.model.reviewer_b
FAST_MODEL        = harness.model.fast
IMPLEMENTER_MODEL = harness.model.implementer

# Thinking — Pi: embedded in the model string above (no separate setting)

# Agents
IMPLEMENTER_AGENT = harness.agent.implementer
REVIEWER_AGENT    = harness.agent.reviewer
```

Skills reference `harness.model.<role>`, `harness.agent.<role>`, and `harness.thinking.<role>`.
For a generic `agent: "reviewer"` dispatch, explicitly pass
`harness.model.reviewer_a`; do not rely on the builtin agent default. Never
substitute an unrelated role's model for a missing binding: if a role has no
binding, omit `model`
so the builtin inherits this session's model, and report the gap.
Never hardcode model names or agent identifiers.

Other skills load this skill with one line:

```markdown
**REQUIRED REFERENCE:** Load and use the `harness` skill for subagent dispatch, agent names, and user prompt syntax.
```

### Capabilities and Tools

| Property | pi |
| ---------- | ---- |
| `harness.tool.user_prompt` | `ask_user_question` |
| `harness.path.skills` | `plugins/.../skills/` |
| `harness.capability.worktree` | `git` (git worktree) |




---

## Part 2: Dispatch & User Prompts

### Subagent Dispatch — Mode Selection

The dispatch tool has two modes. Pick exactly one — never mix parameters.

| Mode | Use when | Key parameters |
|------|----------|----------------|
| **SINGLE** | One agent, one task | `agent`, `task`, `model` |
| **WORKFLOW** | Multiple agents, parallel/sequential | Harness dispatch form (below): one entry per agent |


**Correct — SINGLE mode:** invoke the `subagent` tool with `agent`, `task`,
and `model` arguments. No workflow block is needed and the call is never
documentation.

**Correct — WORKFLOW mode (parallel with a same-turn completion barrier):**

A dispatch needs **two separate acts** in one reply. (1) Write this as the
**one** `js workflow` code block, opening the fence at the start of a line (no
indentation). (2) Invoke the `subagent` tool with `workflow: true` and
`async: true` as a **real tool call**.

Writing `subagent(...)` in a code fence, an inline span, or prose produces
documentation only: it starts nothing, returns no workflow ID, and leaves every
child unstarted while the reply still looks correct. Reproducing the shape of an
example is not dispatching.

The reply text payload:

```js workflow
const results = await runs.all([
  { key: "a", agent: "implementer", task: "Do X", model: "${harness.model.implementer}" },
  { key: "b", agent: "implementer", task: "Do Y", model: "${harness.model.implementer}" }
]);
return results;
```

Then invoke the `subagent` tool with `workflow: true` and `async: true`. It
returns a workflow ID. A fenced `subagent(...)` line is not that call.

`runs.all` starts both entries in parallel. `async: true` follows the Pi
workflow protocol; the Completion barriers rule below decides whether this turn
waits on that ID or ends and waits natively.


### Dispatch by Harness

**Pi** — apply the Completion barriers rule below before the turn ends;
`runs.all` still runs all entries in parallel. A dispatch needs **two separate
acts** in one reply: (1) write this as the **one** `js workflow` code block,
opening the fence at the start of a line (no indentation); (2) invoke the
`subagent` tool with `workflow: true` and `async: true` as a **real tool call**.

Writing `subagent(...)` in a code fence, an inline span, or prose produces
documentation only — it starts nothing and returns no workflow ID. Reproducing
the shape of an example is not dispatching.

The reply text payload:

```js workflow
const results = await runs.all([
  { key: "reviewer-a", agent: "reviewer", task: "<prompt>", model: "${harness.model.reviewer_a}" },
  { key: "reviewer-b", agent: "reviewer", task: "<prompt>", model: "${harness.model.reviewer_b}" }
]);
return results;
```

Then invoke the `subagent` tool with `workflow: true` and `async: true`. It
returns a workflow ID; apply the Completion barriers rule below to decide
between waiting on it and ending the turn.

#### No workflow ID means the dispatch did NOT happen

| What you observe | Meaning | Required action |
| ----------------- | --------- | ----------------- |
| Tool returned a workflow ID | Launched | `bg_wait` that exact ID before the turn ends (chain step) |
| Tool returned an error | Not launched | Fix the cause, re-invoke the tool |
| No tool result in your turn | **Not launched** — you emitted text | Re-invoke the tool; do not proceed |
| You cannot name the workflow ID | **Not launched** | Re-invoke the tool; do not report success |

Never `bg_wait` a placeholder, guessed, or empty ID. Never report a child as
dispatched, running, or started without a workflow ID from the tool. If repeated
invocations return no ID, stop and tell the user the launch failed — a silent
no-op lets collection and every later chain step run against work that does not
exist.

Key rules:

- `async: true` follows the Pi protocol; `runs.all` remains parallel.
- In a chain step, exact-run `bg_wait` before the turn ends is the completion
  barrier; standalone work waits natively.
- Between launch and the barrier, do not send a progress-only response, invoke
  another skill, or let the chain step end.
- After waiting, inspect terminal status and collect every expected result.
- Re-dispatch individual reviewers on `failed`/`cancelled` before de-duplication.
